withheld.headline: ‘They searched my bag, and my Israeli passport was inside’: An extraordinary journey through Saudi Arabia
withheld.evidence: The religious police officers began rummaging through his bag. Hidden deep inside an inner pocket was the last thing he wanted anyone in Saudi Arabia to find: his Israeli passport. "They caught me in Medina, the city sacred to Muslims," adventurer Adam Jano, a resident of the northern Israeli community of Klil, told ynet. "They're not particularly pleasant people. They started searching through my things, and I was an idiot for bringing it with me," he recalled. "I had to move between hotels, so I thought, fine, I'll take it along. I hid it, and luckily they didn't see it." The encounter took place in the courtyard of the Prophet Muhammad's Mosque in Medina, one of Islam's holiest cities. "The religious police asked me, 'Are you Muslim?' I said, 'No, I'm not Muslim.' Then they started saying, 'Give us your bag.' They began searching, and my heart just sank." Jano checked into one of the region's luxury resorts and discovered a swimming pool in the middle of the desert, gourmet restaurants, golf carts and impeccable five-star service. It was incredibly moving." Jano's search for Jewish roots in Saudi Arabia also brought him to an abandoned Jewish cemetery in the city of Al-Hofuf. "You imagine you're going to see gravestones, but all there was was this white sand that had been packed down by sandstorms," he recalled. "You're actually walking over the graves and can't see anything because the desert has covered everything. But the local Muslims still respect the place and don't build on it.

withheld.headline: Greenpeace calls for ban on “dead waste” textile imports into Ghana | Ghana News Agency
withheld.evidence: Ghana's preferred news source: Accurate, Credible, Objective, Timely Accra, Oct. 8, GNA – Greenpeace Africa, an independent environmental campaigning organisation, has called on the Government to ban the importation of what it calls “dead waste” textiles into the country, describing them as clothing that cannot be reused, repurposed or resold. The call follows a brand audit of some 201 discarded garments collected from James Town Beach, Kantamanto Market and Agbogbloshie in Accra, which identified labels of global fashion brands including H&M, Primark, Marks & Spencer (M&S) and Next, as major contributors to Ghana’s textile waste. The organisation said the growing volume of discarded clothing in Accra highlighted the need for action both at the source of production and at Ghana’s borders. Presenting the audit findings on Wednesday in Accra, as part of its campaign on “waste colonialism” and the environmental and economic effects of the global fast-fashion industry, Ms Hellen Kahaso Dena, Project Lead for the Plastics Project and Fast Fashion at Greenpeace Africa, said the organisation’s investigations across Accra showed that textile waste was accumulating at several locations, including Kantamanto Market, James Town Beach and Agbogbloshie. She said the problem needed to be addressed by reducing excessive production by global fashion companies and ensuring that only clothing capable of being reused entered Ghana. “We want to tackle this problem at the source, and the source of this problem is the overproduction,” Ms Dena said. Ms Dena explained that while Greenpeace was not calling for a complete ban on second-hand clothing imports as the trade provided livelihoods for many Ghanaians, it could also not be left unchecked. He also expressed concern about plastic and microplastic pollution arising from synthetic fibres used in many garments. Mr Quashie-Idun cited Greenpeace’s 2024 report, “Fast Fashion, Slow Poison”, which found that 89 per cent of 164 discarded garments tested at three dumpsites in the Greater Accra Region contained synthetic fibres. The petition called for a ban on unusable textile waste, transparent grading and trading practices, stronger producer responsibility mechanisms, investment in Ghana’s textile industry and support for traditional craftsmanship, repair and reuse. “We don’t want to see a total ban on import here. The quality needs to be better and we have to stop the overproduction,” she said. Head Office Location Opp.

withheld.headline: Dixcove Fishermen Reject Offshore Gold Exploration
withheld.evidence: Fishermen at Dixcove have rejected GoldCoast Resource Corporation's bid to explore for gold offshore, saying the ocean that sustains their families cannot be handed over without their consent. For generations, the waters off Dixcove in the Ahanta West Municipality have put food on tables and paid school fees for families along Ghana's Western Region coastline. Now, fishermen there say that lifeline is under threat from a proposed offshore gold exploration project they were never properly consulted about. Fishermen in the coastal town have rejected plans by GoldCoast Resource Corporation to explore for gold offshore, arguing the venture could endanger their livelihoods and damage the marine environment, according to the Ghanaian Times . The fishermen insist the ocean remains their traditional source of food and income, and that any decision affecting its use must involve the communities whose survival depends on it. Their position emerged on Tuesday during an engagement organised by Friends of the Nation (FON), a civil society organisation that works on coastal and marine conservation issues, the Ghanaian Times reports. The meeting brought together stakeholders at Dixcove to discuss the proposed exploration and examine its possible effects on fishing grounds, marine ecosystems and the wider coastal economy. According to the newspaper, the engagement was designed to promote the protection of Ghana's ocean resources, uphold the rights of fishermen, and safeguard the sustainability of livelihoods along the coast. Any disruption to fishing grounds — whether through exploration activity, pollution, or restricted access to the sea — could ripple through household incomes, local fish markets, and food security in communities that have few alternative sources of livelihood. Friends of the Nation's continued engagement with coastal stakeholders suggests the organisation intends to keep pressing the issue, but no specific dates for further action, hearings, or government responses have been disclosed. withheld.headline: A century after it was taken, ancestral tipi cover returns to Kawacatoose First Nation
withheld.evidence: Cree community in Saskatchewan brings home their Ancestor sîpiskwêsîkan’s painted fabric from Smithsonian in ‘Washington, D.C.’ Brittany Boschman, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter Those were okimâw (Chief) Cory Dustyhorn’s words when he first touched the tipi cover connected to his great-great-great-grandfather, sîpiskwêsîkan. After a century away from Kawacatoose First Nation , the ancestral item has returned to the Cree community. Community and family members gathered around the tipi cover after it was brought back from the Smithsonian Institution’s National Museum of the American Indian in “Washington, D.C.” “When I first touched it, I just felt so emotional,” Dustyhorn said. “I was thinking of all those that are gone on before me.” He thought about his parents, grandparents and ancestors — who preserved the history of the item through generations. Until the First Nation can build a permanent museum or cultural centre to house it safely, they plan to bring it home each year. Andrew Miller, an associate professor at the First Nations University of Canada, helped the Dustyhorn family locate the item and communicate with the Smithsonian. It also requires returning ancestral belongings and supporting communities as they restore cultural teachings. Dustyhorn said the return also highlights the need for stronger support from governments and museums — for all Indigenous communities hoping to recover what was taken away from them. “They talk about truth and reconciliation,” he said.
